rows.name: Muhammad Taqi Usmani
rows.key_contribution: Chaired AAOIFI Shariah Board; 2008 ruling that ~85% of sukuk non-compliant.
rows.bio_full: Muhammad Taqi Usmani was born in October 1943 in Deoband, in what was then British India, according to Wikipedia. Wikipedia says he completed the Alimiyyah course at Darul Uloom Karachi in 1959 and a specialisation in fiqh and fatwa-giving there in 1961. He then took a BA at the University of Karachi in 1964. A law degree from the same university followed in 1967. In 1970 he gained an MA in Arabic from the University of the Punjab. From 1977 to 1981 he sat on Pakistan's Council of Islamic Ideology. He was a judge of the Federal Shariat Court from 1981 to 1982. From 1982 to 2002 he served on the Shariat Appellate Bench of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Arab News reported that as a judge he took part in a ruling on usury. Wikipedia describes him as vice president of Darul Uloom Karachi, where he also teaches hadith. Meezan Bank's website says he chairs the Centre for Islamic Economics, a division of Jamia Darul Uloom Karachi. Wikipedia says he chairs the Shariah Board of AAOIFI, the Bahrain-based standard-setting body for Islamic financial institutions. A 2014 Arab News report gave his AAOIFI title as chairman of its Shari'ah Standard Council. Gulf News reported in June 2008 that he had said about 85 per cent of sukuk did not comply with Islamic law. The reason reported was the use of repurchase agreements, which guarantee the face value of the sukuk at maturity. The same report says AAOIFI's scholars met in February 2008 and confirmed the ban on such repurchase agreements. Sukuk that had already been issued were treated as valid. Arab News reported that the February 2008 meeting in Bahrain required tradable sukuk to give their holders ownership of the underlying assets. In 2014 the Islamic Development Bank named him joint winner, with Rodney Wilson, of its prize in Islamic banking and finance. The reasons reported included his writings and his part in bringing Islamic finance into the teaching of traditional religious schools. The report also said he had advised and supervised Islamic financial institutions in the Muslim world, Europe and the United States. Wikipedia credits him with 143 books in Urdu, Arabic and English. The titles it names include An Introduction to Islamic Finance and a six-volume commentary on Sahih Muslim. Wikipedia lists Jordan's Order of Independence among his honours, dated 2010. It also lists Pakistan's Sitara-i-Imtiaz, dated 2019. Wikipedia says he has been president of Wifaq ul Madaris Al-Arabia, the board of Deobandi seminaries in Pakistan, since September 2021.

rows.name: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi
rows.key_contribution: Two-tier mudarabah banking model; King Faisal Prize 1982.
rows.controversy: Criticized modern Islamic banking as too close to conventional.
rows.bio_full: Mohammad Nejatullah Siddiqi was born on 21 August 1931 in Gorakhpur, India. He studied at Aligarh Muslim University, where he took his MA and PhD. Wikipedia adds that he also studied at Rampur and Azamgarh. At Aligarh he taught economics as an associate professor. He was also Professor of Islamic Studies there. From 1978 to 2000 he was Professor of Economics at King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah. The King Faisal Prize page records him as a member of AAOIFI in Bahrain in 1999. In 2001 he was President of the International Association for Islamic Economics. In the same year he was a Fellow at the Center of Near Eastern Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles. He was a visiting scholar at the Islamic Development Bank in 2002. In 2006 he held a distinguished professorship at the International Islamic University in Kuala Lumpur. Wikipedia also records him as Professor Emeritus in the Department of Management Studies at Aligarh. It adds that he was Chief Patron of the Indian Centre for Islamic Finance in New Delhi. The prize page counts 14 books in English, 13 in Urdu and 7 in Arabic. The books it singles out are Banking Without Interest, The Theory of Ownership in Islam, Role of the State in the Economy: An Islamic Perspective, Dialogue in Islamic Economics, and Modern Writings in Islamic Economics: Selected Essays. Wikipedia says Banking Without Interest went through 27 editions between 1973 and 2000. Other titles listed by Wikipedia include Recent Theories of Profit (1971), Economic Enterprise in Islam (1972), Muslim Economic Thinking (1981), Partnership and Profit-Sharing in Islamic Law (1985) and Insurance in an Islamic Economy (1985). He received the King Faisal Prize in Islamic Studies in 1982, when the prize topic was contemporary economic problems from an Islamic perspective. The prize page says the award was for work that treated present-day economic questions within Islamic guidance. In 2003 he received the Shah Waliullah Award in New Delhi for his work in Islamic economics. He died on 12 November 2022. Wikipedia gives the place of death as California in the United States.

rows.name: Muhammad Umer Chapra
rows.key_contribution: Towards a Just Monetary System; Islamic monetary theory.
rows.verified_note: web-checked 2026-07-04: Died 13 Jun 2026, Saudi Arabia (IsDBI, Arab News, Wikipedia). Was 'living'.
rows.bio_full: Muhammad Umer Chapra was born on 1 February 1933 in Mumbai, then called Bombay. The King Faisal Prize page says he took his bachelor's and master's degrees at Karachi University in 1956. He gained a PhD from the University of Minnesota in 1961. Wikipedia says the doctorate was in economics and sociology. He worked as a research assistant at Minnesota. He then taught economics as an associate professor at universities in Wisconsin and Kentucky. In 1965 he moved to Saudi Arabia to take an economic adviser's post at the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency, the country's central bank. Arab News says he was among the earliest Pakistanis to move to the Kingdom. The prize page says he advised the Saudi monetary authority for 34 years. Arab News says he is credited with helping to shape the central bank in its early years. Afterwards he was a research adviser at the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah. Saudi Arabia gave him citizenship for his services to the country. His books include Towards a Just Monetary System (1985), Islam and the Economic Challenge (1992) and The Future of Economics: An Islamic Perspective (2004). Wikipedia also lists Muslim Civilization: The Causes of Decline and the Need for Reform. Arab News puts his output at about 15 books and monographs and more than 90 articles. Wikipedia records that he received the Islamic Development Bank Award for Islamic Economics in 1989. He received the King Faisal Prize in Islamic Studies in 1990, when the topic was financial dealings in Islamic law. The prize page ties the award to the Arabic edition of Towards a Just Monetary System. It says the book followed a sound method and showed a deep grasp of the bases of Sharia. Wikipedia adds a gold medal from the President of Pakistan in 1995. He died in Makkah on 13 June 2026, aged 93. Arab News reported that funeral prayers were to be held at the Grand Mosque in Makkah, with burial at Al Ma'la Cemetery.

rows.name: Monzer Kahf
rows.key_contribution: Islamic finance contracts, waqf, zakat economics.
rows.bio_full: Monzer Kahf is described on a Canadian teaching site as a Syrian American professor of Islamic economics and finance. He took a BA in business at the University of Damascus in June 1962. His own website says he received the President of Syria's award for the best graduating university student that year. He taught for a year at the university's School of Business, from 1962 to 1963. From 1963 to 1971 he worked as an auditor at the state audit office in Damascus. In 1967 he earned a higher diploma in social and economic planning from the UN Institute of Planning. He has been a certified public accountant in Syria since 1968. He was a teaching assistant in economics at the University of Utah from 1971 to 1975. He received his PhD in economics from the University of Utah in 1975. From 1975 to 1981 he was Director of Finance at the Islamic Society of North America in Plainfield, Indiana. In the same years he managed the National Zakah Fund and the Islamic Cooperative Fund. From 1981 to 1985 he worked in New York as a financial and investment consultant. He joined the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah in 1985 as a research economist and stayed until 1999. He headed the institute's research division from 1989 to 1991. He became a senior research economist there. Since 1999 he has worked from California as a private consultant, trainer and lecturer in Islamic banking, finance and economics. In 2004 to 2005 he taught Islamic economics and banking in the graduate programme at Yarmouk University in Jordan. A 2018 conference page lists him as Professor of Islamic Finance and Islamic Economics. The same page says he has been a consultant on Islamic finance to the International Monetary Fund. He is a collaborating expert at the Islamic Fiqh Academy of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. He has sat on several of its technical committees on Sharia, finance and economics. His website counts 28 books and booklets in English and Arabic. It also counts more than 100 articles and papers. The research project it names is a book on the theory of Islamic banking. He received the Islamic Development Bank Prize for Islamic Economics in 2001.

rows.bio_full: Sami Hamoud was a Jordanian economist. He studied in Egypt in the 1970s, where he took part in the academic debate on finance that follows Islamic law. He then went back to Jordan to put the ideas into practice. Oxford Business Group says the founding of Jordan's first Islamic bank was largely his doing. He obtained financial backing from members of the Saudi royal family. He answered the government's worries about licensing a fully Islamic bank by lobbying in person and through a preparatory committee. In May 1977 the prime minister's office issued a decision allowing the bank. Jordan Islamic Bank opened in 1978. Wikipedia's article on murabaha, citing Mahmoud El-Gamal's book Islamic Finance (2006), credits a Sami Humud with developing the deferred-payment sale used by Islamic banks.

rows.name: Wahbah al-Zuhayli
rows.key_contribution: al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu; fiqh encyclopedia.
rows.bio_full: Wahbah al-Zuhayli was born in 1932 in Dair Atiah, Syria, according to Wikipedia. Wikipedia says he studied Sharia in Damascus for six years and finished first in his class in 1952. He graduated from al-Azhar University in Cairo in 1956. He took a bachelor's degree at Ain Shams University in 1957. A master's degree in law from Cairo University followed in 1959. He gained his doctorate in law in 1963 with a thesis on the effects of war in Islamic jurisprudence. A news report on his death also says his doctorate was from Cairo University. He taught at Damascus University from 1963 and became a professor there in 1975. Wikipedia says he was a visiting professor at the University of Benghazi from 1972 to 1974 and at the University of the United Arab Emirates from 1984 to 1989. He advised Islamic financial companies on Islamic law. Wikipedia credits him with more than 160 books. His work on Islamic law and its evidences, al-Fiqh al-Islami wa Adillatuhu, is described there as an eight-volume survey. His commentary on the Qur'an, al-Tafsir al-Munir, is given there as 17 volumes. He also wrote a two-volume work on Islamic legal theory. Wikipedia lists Financial Transactions in Islamic Jurisprudence, a two-volume work on present-day Islamic business law. He was a member of the Islamic Fiqh Academy in Jeddah. A news report adds fiqh councils in Makkah, India, Sudan and the United States. He signed the Amman Message. The same news report says he won a Muslim world book of the year award in 1995. He died in Damascus in August 2015. A tribute by Zaid Shakir, who knew him in Damascus, names the law survey and the Qur'an commentary as his main works.

rows.name: Yusuf al-Qaradawi
rows.key_contribution: Fiqh al-Zakat; permissibility rulings.
rows.controversy: Designated terrorist-linked by several states; politically divisive.
rows.bio_full:
Yusuf al-Qaradawi (Arabic: يوسف القرضاوي, romanized: Yūsuf al-Qaraḍāwī; or Yusuf al-Qardawi; 9 September 1926 – 26 September 2022) was an Egyptian Islamic scholar based in Doha, Qatar, and chairman of the International Union of Muslim Scholars. His influences included Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Qayyim, Sayyid Rashid Rida, Hassan al-Banna, Abul Hasan Ali Hasani Nadwi, Abul A'la Maududi and Naeem Siddiqui. He was best known for his programme الشريعة والحياة, al-Sharīʿa wa al-Ḥayāh ("Sharia and Life"), broadcast on Al Jazeera, which had an estimated audience of 40–60 million worldwide. He was also known for IslamOnline, a website he helped for establishment in 1997 and for which he served as chief religious scholar.
Al-Qaradawi published more than 120 books, including The Lawful and the Prohibited in Islam and Islam: The Future Civilization. He also received eight international prizes for his contributions to Islamic scholarship, and was considered one of the most influential Islamic scholars living. Al-Qaradawi had a prominent role within the intellectual leadership of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Egyptian political organization, although he repeatedly stated that he was no longer a member and twice (in 1976 and 2004) turned down offers for the leadership of the organization.
Al-Qaradawi was sometimes described as a "moderate Islamist". Some of his views, such as his condoning of Palestinian suicide bombings against Israelis, caused reactions from governments in the West: he was refused an entry visa to the United Kingdom in 2008, and barred from entering France in 2012.

Biography

In Egypt
Al-Qaradawi was born on 9 September 1926 in Saft Turab rural village in the Nile Delta, now in Gharbia Governorate, Egypt, into a poor family of devout Muslim peasants. He became an orphan at the age of two, when he lost his father. Following his father's death, he was raised by his mother and uncle. He read and memorized the entire Quran before he was ten years old.
He then joined the Institute of Religious Studies at Tanta, and graduated after nine years of study. While in Tanta, Al-Qaradawi first encountered Hassan al Banna, the founder of the Muslim Brotherhood, when al Banna gave a lecture at his school. Al-Qaradawi wrote of the lasting impact of this encounter, describing al Banna as "brilliantly radiating, as if his words were revelation or live coals from the light of prophecy."
After graduating from the Institute of Religious Studies he moved on to study Islamic Theology at the Al-Azhar University in Cairo, from which he graduated in 1953. He earned a diploma in Arabic Language and Literature in 1958 at the Advanced Arabic Studies Institute. He enrolled in the graduate program in the Department of Quran and Sunnah Sciences of the Faculty of Religion's Fundamentals (Usul al-Din), and graduated with a master's degree in Quranic studies in 1960. In 1962, he was sent by Al-Azhar University to Qatar to head the Qatari Secondary Institute of Religious Studies. He completed his PhD thesis titled Zakah and its effect on solving social problems in 1973 with First Merit and was awarded his PhD degree from Al-Azhar.
His connection with the Muslim Brotherhood led to imprisonment under King Farouq in 1949, then three more times during the term of President Gamal Abdul Nasser. He left Egypt for Qatar in 1961, and did not return until the overthrow of the military regime by the 2011 Egyptian Revolution.

Based in Qatar
In 1977, he laid the foundation for the Faculty of Shari'ah and Islamic Studies at the University of Qatar and became the faculty's dean. In the same year he founded the Centre of Seerah and Sunna Research. He also served at Egypt's Institute of Imams under the Ministry of Religious Endowments as supervisor before moving back to Doha as Dean of the Islamic Department at the Faculties of Shariah and Education in Qatar, where he continued until 1990. His next appointment was in Algeria as Chairman of the Scientific Council of Islamic University and Higher Institutions in 1990–91. He returned to Qatar once more as Director of the Seerah and Sunnah Center at Qatar University.
In 1997, Al-Qaradawi helped found the European Council for Fatwa and Research, a council of important and influential Muslim scholars dedicated to researching and writing fatwas in support of Western Muslim minority communities based in Ireland, and he served as its head. He also served as the chairman of International Union for Muslim Scholars (IUMS).
In the wake of the 2011 Revolution he returned to Egypt for the first time since leaving in 1961.
Al-Qaradawi was a principal shareholder and former Sharia adviser to Bank Al-Taqwa. On 2 August 2010, the bank was removed from a list of entities and individuals associated with Al Qaeda maintained by the United Nations Security Council.
Al-Qaradawi finished third in a 2008 poll on who was the world's leading public intellectual. The poll, Top 100 Public Intellectuals, was conducted among readers of Prospect Magazine (UK) and Foreign Policy (United States).

2011 return to Egypt
After the 2011 Egyptian Revolution, Qaradawi made his first public appearance in Egypt after 1981. In Tahrir Square, he led Friday prayers on 18 February, addressing an audience estimated to exceed two million Egyptians. It began with an address of "O Muslims and Copts", referring to Egypt's Coptic Christian minority instead of the customary opening for Islamic Friday sermons "O Muslims". He was reported to have said, "Egyptian people are like the genie who came out of the lamp and who have been in prison for 30 years." He also demanded the release of political prisoners in Egyptian prisons, praised the Copts for protecting Muslims in their Friday prayer, and called for the new military rulers to quickly restore civilian rule. In the sermon, Qaradawi called for the immediate release of political prisoners, the dissolution of the cabinet of Mubarak loyalists, and an end to the economic blockade of Gaza.
Brookings Institution member Shadi Hamid said that Qaradawi was in the mainstream of Egyptian society, and that he also had appeal among Egyptians who are not Islamist. He described the sermon as "nonsectarian" and "broadly political". In the Jerusalem Post, Barry Rubin wrote that although he was seen as a moderate by some in the West, he supported the straight Islamist line. Qaradawi was seen as a danger by Rubin because he was a charismatic thinker who could easily mobilise the masses. The author was concerned that Qaradawi would take over Egypt and that this would have had negative consequences for Israel.
On 21 February 2011, Qaradawi issued a fatwa, which is a religious ruling, permitting the killing of Muammar Gaddafi. This was in response to Gaddafi's plans to kill protesters in Libya. He also called on Libyan ambassadors around the world to distance themselves from Gaddafi's government.

Death
On the afternoon of 26 September 2022, Qaradawi died in Qatar at the age of 96. After a funeral service attended by thousands of people including the deputy emir of Qatar Abdullah bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, and other Qatari and foreign officials at Imam Mohammed bin Abdul Wahab Mosque, Qardawi was buried at Mesaimeer Cemetery in Doha.

Views and statements

Religious and sectarian views

Extremism
Al-Qaradawi wrote on the danger of extremist groups of Islam, in his dissertation on the subject Islamic Awakening between Rejection and Extremism. This dissertation discusses the phenomenon of religious extremism among Muslim youth. He discusses the reasons why young Muslims may resort to extremism, and argues that many of these reasons are due to the hypocrisy and self-contradictions of older Muslims.

rows.name: Mustafa al-Zarqa
rows.key_contribution: Modern theory of Islamic contracts and insurance permissibility.
rows.bio_full: Mustafa Ahmad al-Zarqa was born in Aleppo, Syria. The Turkish Diyanet encyclopaedia explains that official records show 1904 as his birth year because his age was raised for a school requirement. He memorised the Qur'an as a child in Aleppo. He finished high school at the top of his class. In 1933 he graduated first from both the law and the arts faculties of the Syrian University in Damascus. He later earned a diploma in Islamic law from Fuad I University in Cairo, which the encyclopaedia dates to 1947. He practised as a lawyer in Aleppo for about ten years. Arab News says he began lecturing at the University of Damascus in 1944 and retired from it in 1966. He was elected to the Syrian parliament. He served as minister of justice and of religious endowments, a post the encyclopaedia dates to 1956. He held the same two ministries again in 1961. After Syria and Egypt united in 1958 he chaired the commission that drafted a shared personal status law. From 1966 he supervised the preparation of an encyclopaedia of Islamic law in Kuwait. He taught at the Faculty of Sharia of the University of Jordan from 1971 until 1989. In 1981 the Arab League named him to a committee charged with drafting a unified Arab civil law. He sat for many years on the Islamic Fiqh Council in Makkah. The encyclopaedia names al-Fiqh al-Islami fi Thawbihi al-Jadid as his best-known book on Islamic law. Arab News describes his three-volume al-Madkhal al-Fiqhi al-Amm as a general introduction to Islamic law. His book al-Madkhal ila Nazariyyat al-Iltizam deals with the theory of obligations in Islamic law. The King Faisal Prize page counts twelve books, among them works on the law of endowments and on insurance contracts. He held that insurance is allowed in principle, a view that started a long debate. Arab News places him among the earliest scholars to give that ruling. He set the view out in a book on the insurance system. His collected fatwas deal largely with economic life and banking. He received the King Faisal Prize in Islamic Studies, which the prize's own page dates to 1984, on the topic of general theory in Islamic jurisprudence. The encyclopaedia adds that he also received an award from the Islamic Development Bank. He died in Riyadh on 3 July 1999.

rows.key_contribution: Foundational works on Islamic jurisprudence and contracts.
rows.bio_full: Muhammad Abu Zahra was born on 29 March 1898 in El-Mahalla El-Kubra, in Egypt's Nile Delta. In 1913 he entered the Ahmadi mosque school in Tanta. In 1916 he enrolled at the School of Sharia Judges in Cairo. Wikipedia says he had the highest mark in his province in that school's entrance examination. He completed the Dar al-Ulum college as an external student in 1927. The same year he began teaching Arabic and Islamic law. He then taught in secondary schools in Sohag and Cairo. In November 1934 he moved to the Faculty of Law at Fuad I University, now Cairo University, where he later taught Islamic law and headed the department. He retired from the Faculty of Law in 1958 and continued to teach there. He was elected to the Islamic Research Academy in February 1962. He acted as rapporteur for commissions that worked on codifying Islamic law. His book on legal theory, Usul al-Fiqh (1957), is described by the Turkish Diyanet encyclopaedia as among the early modern works in that field. He wrote on crime and punishment in Islamic law using modern legal terms. He wrote a series of lives of the founders of the law schools, including Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Wikipedia also names his history of the Islamic schools of thought. He wrote on personal status law, endowments and property. The encyclopaedia lists a study of his on riba, Buhuth fi al-Riba, without setting out its argument. On insurance, he held that the dealings of private insurance are not allowed. In 1969 he strongly criticised a draft personal status law. He held, against the four schools, that three divorces spoken at one time count as one. His commentary on the Qur'an, Zahrat al-Tafasir, was unfinished when he died. He died on 11 April 1974.

He was the founder and chairman of the holding company Dallah Albaraka. He was also the founder and chairman of Al Baraka Banking Group. He set up Al Baraka Investment and Development as a holding company. In 1979 he set up the Islamic Arab Insurance Company, a takaful (Islamic insurance) firm. He funded research bodies, among them the Islamic Economics Research Centre at King Abdulaziz University. He also founded the Saleh Kamel Centre for Islamic Economy at Al-Azhar University in Cairo. The yearly Albaraka Symposium on Islamic Economics, which he sponsored, had by 2010 issued over 150 rulings used in Islamic financial research. He helped to set up the standard-setting body AAOIFI in 1991. At the time of his death he was Deputy Chairman of the AAOIFI Board of Trustees. He chaired the General Council for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions. He was president of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture. He chaired the Jeddah Chamber of Commerce and Industry. He sat on the President's Advisory Panel of the Islamic Development Bank. Outside finance he owned the ART television network. In 2010 Malaysia gave him its Royal Award for Islamic Finance. Wikipedia records that he was arrested in Saudi Arabia on 4 November 2017 during an anti-corruption campaign. He died on 18 May 2020, aged 79. AAOIFI recorded the date in the Islamic calendar as the 26th of Ramadan.

rows.name: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr
rows.key_contribution: Iqtisaduna (Our Economics); Islamic economic doctrine.
rows.bio_full: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr was an Iraqi Shia cleric and thinker, born in 1935 in al-Kazimiya. He finished his religious training in the seminaries of Najaf, where Wikipedia names Abu al-Qasim al-Khoei and Muhsin al-Hakim among his teachers. Wikipedia describes him as the thinker behind the founding ideas of the Islamic Dawa Party. His book on philosophy, Falsafatuna (Our Philosophy), came out in 1959. His economics book, Iqtisaduna (Our Economy), was written in Arabic in 1960 and 1961. An English translation was issued by the Iranian government in 1982. The book examines Marxism and capitalism and then sets out an Islamic system as a third choice. He treated Islamic economics as a doctrine in its own right and not as a mixture of the other two systems. On ownership he held that private and public property alike come from God. He also wrote a work on banking without interest, listed in English as Usury-free Banking in Islam. According to Wikipedia this banking work grew from a request by the government of Kuwait for a study of how its oil wealth could be handled on Islamic lines, and the page says it still underlies present-day Islamic banks. He was jailed several times under the Baath government. He issued a religious ruling that barred Muslims from joining the ruling Baath party. After protests in 1977 he was confined to his home. He was arrested for the last time on 5 April 1980, together with his sister Amina, known as Bint al-Huda. Both were tortured and killed by the government of Saddam Hussein; Wikipedia gives the date of his death as 9 April 1980.

He twice received the Isma'il al-Faruqi Award for Academic Excellence at the International Islamic University Malaysia, in 1995 and 1997. rows.bio_full: Abdul Sattar Abu Ghuddah was a Syrian jurist and Shariah adviser to Islamic banks, born in Aleppo on 28 January 1940. He studied Shariah and law at Damascus University. He gained a master's degree in Shariah in 1966 at Al-Azhar University. He also took a master's degree in hadith. His doctorate, in comparative jurisprudence, was awarded by Al-Azhar in 1975. In 1966 he taught jurisprudence at a religious institute in Riyadh. He then worked as an expert and rapporteur on the encyclopaedia of Islamic law produced by Kuwait's Ministry of Awqaf, a post Arabic Wikipedia says he held until 1990. In 2006 he chaired the Shariah board of Syria International Islamic Bank. He helped to found a Shariah advisory firm in Dubai. His books include a study of options in contracts, al-Khiyar wa-atharuhu fi al-uqud. He died in Montreal, Canada, on 23 October 2020. A book chapter of his sets out the foundations of risk-sharing finance from an Islamic view. In 2003 he received the Islamic Development Bank's annual prize for research in Islamic economics. rows.bio_full: Timur Kuran was born in New York City in 1954, according to Wikipedia. His family moved to Istanbul in 1969. He finished school at Robert College in Istanbul in 1973. He studied economics at Princeton University and graduated in 1977. He took his doctorate in economics at Stanford University in 1982. From 1982 to 2007 he taught at the University of Southern California. There he held the King Faisal professorship in Islamic Thought and Culture from 1993. He has been a member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He was also the John Olin Visiting Professor at the University of Chicago's Graduate School of Business. In 2007 he moved to Duke University, where he is Professor of Economics and Political Science. At Duke he also holds the Gorter Family chair in Islamic Studies. He introduced the term preference falsification in an article of 1987. His book on that idea is Private Truths, Public Lies (1995). His book Islam and Mammon: The Economic Predicaments of Islamism was published by Princeton University Press, which lists a 2004 copyright. In it he argues that the doctrine of Islamic economics does not hold together and has little bearing on present economic problems. He holds that its real aim has been to build a separate Islamic identity against cultural globalization. On Islamic banks, set up to avoid interest, he says the firms in practice deal in interest as a matter of routine. He finds that Islamic economics has made no visible difference to efficiency, trust or poverty. Of modern zakat systems he says they mostly move resources around inside the middle class. His 2011 book The Long Divergence argues that Islamic law held back the economy of the Middle East. He also edited a ten-volume work in three languages on seventeenth-century Istanbul. He directs the Association for Analytic Learning about Islam and Muslim Societies. He is a member of the Turkish Academy of Sciences.

rows.bio_full: Khurshid Ahmad was born on 23 March 1932 in Delhi. Wikipedia says his family was Urdu-speaking and moved to Lahore in Pakistan after the partition of 1947. According to Wikipedia he took a first-class BA in economics in 1952. The profile kept by his own institute lists an MA in economics (1955), a law degree (1959) and a second MA (1964), together with honorary doctorates, one of them from Loughborough University in 2003. Wikipedia says he went to the University of Leicester for a doctorate in economics in 1967-68. He was a member of the Jamaat-e-Islami party and later one of its deputy leaders. With Khurram Murad he set up the Islamic Foundation in Leicester. His institute's profile lists him as chairman of the Islamic Foundation from 1978. From August 1978 to April 1979 he was Pakistan's federal minister for planning, development and statistics. In the same period he was deputy chairman of the Planning Commission. He founded the Institute of Policy Studies in Islamabad and is listed as its chairman from 1979. From 1983 to 1987 he chaired the International Institute of Islamic Economics at the International Islamic University. He sat in the Senate of Pakistan from 1985 to 1997 and again from March 2003. Wikipedia says his last Senate term ended in 2012. He also chaired the Markfield Institute of Higher Education. His books in English include Economic Development in an Islamic Framework (1979), Studies in Islamic Economics (1980) and Towards Monetary and Fiscal System of Islam (1981). Wikipedia also lists Islam and the West (1957), Family Life in Islam (1974) and, as editor, Elimination of Riba from the Economy (1994). Wikipedia says his work helped make Islamic economic jurisprudence a subject of academic study. He received the Islamic Development Bank Award for 1408H (1988) for his work in Islamic economics. In 1990 he received the King Faisal International Prize for service to Islam. Pakistan gave him the Nishan-i-Imtiaz, its highest civil award. He died in Leicester on 13 April 2025, aged 93. Dawn reported that he was buried in Leicester. The Islamic Foundation's statement on his death called him its founding chairman and a pioneer in modern Islamic economics. Marmara University's Islamic economics institute issued a notice of condolence that described him in similar terms.

In July 2017 he taught a course in Istanbul on the methodology of Islamic economics. The Auditor-General of Pakistan has placed him in its hall of fame. rows.name: Volker Nienhaus

rows.bio_full: Volker Nienhaus is a German economist, born on 19 July 1951 in Essen. He studied economics at the Ruhr University Bochum from 1970 to 1974. He gained his doctorate in 1979 and his habilitation, the German qualification for a professorship, in 1985, both at Bochum. He was professor of economics at Bochum from 1985 to 1989. He taught at the University of Trier in 1989-90. He then returned to Bochum to hold the chair of economic policy. From 1997 to 1999 he was dean of the economics faculty there. The University of Marburg elected him president on 17 November 2003; he came from outside the university. The university says he led it from 2004 until early 2010. He was formally seen off at a handover ceremony on 22 April 2010, when Katharina Krause took over. One of his research fields is international economic policy, above all that of Arab and Asian countries. In a 2013 lecture at the Qatar Faculty of Islamic Studies in Doha he said Islamic banking could suit any customer, Muslim or not. In the same lecture he said Islamic banking differs little from ordinary banking in its basics, apart from leaving out forbidden products. He gave as its strength that it avoids very high risk and doubtful lines of business. In 2014 he was a visiting professor at the ICMA Centre and was invited to speak at a CFA Institute conference in Jordan on Islamic banking.

A 2013 Euromoney article says he had recently left the professorship. He serves as an expert at the fiqh academies of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Islamic World League. He sits on the Shari'a Board of the Accounting and Auditing Organisation for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI). Euromoney lists his advisory roles at the Dow Jones Islamic indices, HSBC Amanah, Standard Chartered Saadiq and CitiIslamic, among others. A 2010 MEED profile reported that he held more than 60 Shariah board seats. He is on the advisory board of the Harvard Series on Islamic Law. In February 2013 Euromoney gave him its award for Outstanding Contribution to Islamic Finance.

Arabic Wikipedia says he sits on more than seventy Shariah boards, most of them for financial institutions. His books include a study of paper currency, its history and legal ruling. He also wrote on insurance in Islamic law and on Islamic economics, and published a four-volume collection of research papers and fatwas.

rows.name: Muhammad Hamidullah
rows.key_contribution: Early (1930s) writings on Islamic economics & state finance.
rows.bio_full:
Muhammad Hamidullah (19 February 1908 – 17 December 2002) was an Islamic scholar from the princely state of Hyderabad. He wrote dozens of books and hundreds of articles on Islamic science, history and culture.

Early life and education
Hamidullah was born in Hyderabad, the capital city of Hyderabad State, (now Hyderabad, Telangana, India) the youngest amongst three brothers and five sisters. Both his great-grandfather and his grandfather were Islamic scholars who authored commentaries on the Quran.
Hamidullah's father Mufti Abu Mohammad Khalilullah, was a scholar of Islamic jurisprudence, a director of revenue in the government of the Nizam of Hyderabad, and a pioneer in establishing an interest-free banking system in Hyderabad.
Hamidullah obtained the degree of Maulawi Kamil with distinction from Madrasah Nizamiyah, followed by a BA, LLB and MA in international law from Osmania University. He then travelled to Germany and was awarded a D.Phil. by Bonn University in 1932. After serving in the faculty of Bonn as a lecturer in Arabic and Urdu for a short time, he registered at Sorbonne University in France for his second doctorate. He was awarded D.Litt. by the university after 11 months. He taught international law at Osmania University between 1936 and 1946.

Career
In 1948, Hamidullah was appointed by the Nizam as a representative of Hyderabad at the United Nations. Following India's annexation of Hyderabad in 1948, Hamidullah rejected both Pakistani and Indian citizenship. Classed as a Refugee of Hyderabad by the French Government, he lived in exile in Paris. Hamidullah was a research fellow at the French National Centre for Scientific Research from 1954 until he retired in 1978. He also gave regular lectures at Turkish universities during this time.
He is known for his contributions to the research of Hadith, translating the Quran into multiple languages, and for his biography of the Islamic prophet Muhammad in French.
Hamidullah received the Hilal-i-Imtiaz award from the government of Pakistan in 1985. He donated the award's prize money to the Islamic Research Academy at the International Islamic University in Islamabad.

Later life and death
In 1996, Hamidullah moved to Jacksonville, Florida in the United States of America. He died on 17 December 2002.

Literary works
Having "authored over 100 books in English, French, German, Arabic and Urdu, and about 1000 scholarly essays and articles on the various aspects of Islam and related areas", Muhammad Hammidullah's notable publications include :

The Muslim Conduct of State: Being a Treatise on Siyar (Siyar), General Introduction (1941, 1953)
The First Written Constitution in the World (1941, 1975 and 1986)
Islamic Notion of Conflict of Laws (1945)
Die Rezeption Europaischen Rechts in Haiderabad (1953)
Le "Livre des genenalogies" [D'al-Baladuriy by al-Baladuri] (1954)
Introduction to Islam (from 1957 onwards in numerous languages besides English)
Le Saint Coran: Traduction et commentaire de Muhammad Hamidullah avec la collaboration de M. Leturmy (from 1959 onwards)
Muhammad Ibn Ishaq, the Biographer of the Holy Prophet (Pakistan Historical Society) (1967)
Muhammad Rasulullah: A Concise Survey of the Life and Work of the Founder of Islam (1979)

Islam, Philosophy and Science: Four Public Lectures Organized By Unesco June 1980 (editor) (1981)
Why Fast?: Spiritual & Temporal Study of Fast in Islam (Centre Culturel Islamique Paris Series) (1982)
The Prophet's Establishing a State and his Succession (1988)

rows.name: Abul A'la Maududi
rows.key_contribution: Foundational Islamic-economics framework; influenced riba debate.
rows.bio_full:
Abul A'la al-Maududi (Urdu: ابو الاعلیٰ المودودی, romanized: Abū al-Aʿlā al-Mawdūdī; (1903-09-25)25 September 1903 – (1979-09-22)22 September 1979) was an Islamic scholar and the author of Tafhim-ul-Quran, who was active in British India and later, following the partition, in Pakistan. Described by Wilfred Cantwell Smith as "the most systematic thinker of modern Islam", his numerous works, which "covered a range of disciplines such as Qur'anic exegesis, hadith, law, philosophy, and history", were written in Urdu, but then translated into English, Arabic, Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, Burmese, Malayalam and many other languages. He sought to revive Islam, and to propagate what he understood to be "true Islam". He believed that Islam was essential for politics and that it was necessary to institute sharia and preserve Islamic culture similarly as to that during the reign of the Rashidun Caliphs and abandon immorality, from what he viewed as the evils of secularism, nationalism and socialism, which he understood to be the influence of Western imperialism.
He founded the Islamist party Jamaat-e-Islami. At the time of the Indian independence movement, Maududi and the Jamaat-e-Islami actively worked to oppose the partition of India. After it occurred, Maududi and his followers shifted their focus to politicising Islam and generating support for making Pakistan an Islamic state. They are thought to have helped influence General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq to introduce the Islamisation in Pakistan, and to have been greatly strengthened by him after tens of thousands of members and sympathisers were given jobs in the judiciary and civil service during his administration. He was the world's first recipient of the Saudi Arabian King Faisal International Award for his service to Islam in 1979. Maududi was part of establishing and running of Islamic University of Madinah, Saudi Arabia.
Maududi is acclaimed by the Muslim Brotherhood, Islamic Circle of North America, Hamas, Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, and other organisations.

Early life

Background
Maududi was born in the city of Aurangabad in colonial India, then part of the princely state enclave of Hyderabad. He was the youngest of three sons of Ahmad Hasan, a lawyer by profession. His elder brother, Sayyid Abu'l Khayr Maududi (1899–1979), would later become an editor and journalist.
Although his father was only middle-class, he was the descendant of the Chishti. His last name was derived from the first member of the Chishti Silsilah, i.e., Khawajah Syed Qutb ul-Din Maudood Chishti (d. 527 AH). He stated that his paternal family originally moved from Chisht, in modern-day Afghanistan, during the days of Sikandar Lodi (d. 1517), initially settling in the state of Haryana before moving to Delhi later on, and on his mother's side, his ancestor Mirza Tulak, a soldier of Turkic origin, moved into India from Transoxiana around the times of Emperor Aurangzeb (d. 1707), while his maternal grandfather, Mirza Qurban Ali Baig Khan Salik (1816–1881), was a writer and poet in Delhi, a friend of the Urdu poet Ghalib.

Childhood
Until he was nine, Maududi "received religious nurture at the hands of his father and from a variety of teachers employed by him." As his father wanted him to become a maulvi, this education consisted of learning Arabic, Persian, Islamic law and Hadith. He also studied books of mantiq (logic). A precocious child, he translated Qasim Amin's al-Marah al-Jadidah ("The New Woman"), a modernist and feminist work, from Arabic into Urdu at the age of 11. In the field of translation, years later, he also worked on some 3,500 pages from Asfar, the major work of the 17th century Persian-Shi'a mystical thinker Mulla Sadra. His thought would influence Maududi, as "Sadra's notions of rejuvenation of the temporal order, and the necessity of the reign of Islamic law (Shari'ah) for the spiritual ascension of man, found an echo in Maududi's works."

Education
When he was eleven, Maududi was admitted to the eighth class directly in Madrasa Fawqaniyya Mashriqiyya (Oriental High School), Aurangabad, founded by Shibli Nomani, a modernist Islamic scholar trying to synthesise traditional Islamic scholarship with modern knowledge, and which awakened Maududi's long-lasting interest in philosophy (particularly from Thomas Arnold, who also taught the same subject to Muhammad Iqbal) as well as natural sciences, like mathematics, physics, and chemistry. He then moved to a more traditionalist Darul Uloom in Hyderabad. Meanwhile, his father shifted to Bhopal – there Maududi befriended Niaz Fatehpuri, another modernist – where he suffered a severe paralysis attack and died leaving no property or money, forcing his son to abort his education. In 1919 by the time he was 16, and still a modernist in mindset, he moved to Delhi and read books by his distant relative, the reformist Sayyid Ahmad Khan. He also learned English and German to study, intensively, Western philosophy, sociology, and history for full five years: he eventually came up to the conclusion that "ulama' in the past did not endeavor to discover the causes of Europe's rise, and he offered a long list of philosophers whose scholarship had made Europe a world power: Fichte, Hegel, Comte, Mill, Turgot, Adam Smith, Malthus, Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Darwin, Goethe, and Herder, among others. Comparing their contribution to that of Muslims, he concluded that the latter did not reach even 1 percent."

Journalism
Despite his initial publication on electricity in Maarif in 1918 at the age of 15 and his subsequent appointment as editor of the weekly Urdu newspaper Taj in 1920 at the age of 17, he subsequently resumed his studies as an autodidact in 1921. Notably through the influence of certain members of the Jamiat Ulema-e-Hind, he pursued subjects such as philosophical theology and the Dars-e-Nizami curriculum. Maududi obtained ijazahs, which are certificates and diplomas in traditional Islamic learning. However, he abstained from referring to himself as an ''alim in the formal sense, as he perceived the Islamic scholars as regressive, despite some influence from Deobandi on him:He said that he was a middle-class man who had learned through both new and old ways of learning. Maududi concluded that neither the traditional nor the contemporary schools are entirely correct, based on his own inner guidance.
Maududi worked as the editor of al-Jamiah, a newspaper of a group of orthodox Muslims, from 1924 to 1927. This time was critical and had a lot of influence.
Maududi, who has consistently remained committed to securing independence from Britain, began to question the legitimacy of the Indian National Congress and its Muslim allies during the 1920s, when the party adopted a more Hindu identity. He began to gravitate towards Islam, and he believed that democracy would only be viable if the vast majority of Indians were Muslims.
Maududi returned to Hyderabad in 1928 after spending some time in Delhi as a young man.

Political writings
Maududi's works were written and published throughout his life, including influential works from 1933 to 1941. Maududi's most well-known work, and widely considered his most important and influential work, is the Tafhim-ul-Quran (Urdu: تفہيم القرآن‎, Romanised: Towards Understanding the Qur'an), a 6-volume translation and commentary of the Qur'an which Maududi spent many years writing (which was begun in Muharram, 1361 A.H./February 1942).
In 1932, he joined another journal (Tarjuman al-Quran) and from 1932 to 1937 he began to develop his political ideas, and turn towards the cause of Islamic revivalism and Islam as an ideology, over what he called "traditional and hereditary religion". The government of Hyderabad helped support the journal by buying 300 subscriptions which it donated to libraries around India.

rows.name: Fazlur Rahman Malik
rows.key_contribution: Modernist riba reinterpretation.
rows.controversy: Forced to leave Pakistan over views.
rows.bio_full:
Fazlur Rahman Malik ( FAHZ-luhr RAH-mahn MAL-ik; Urdu: فضل الرحمان ملک; September 21, 1919 – July 26, 1988), commonly known as Fazlur Rahman, was a modernist scholar and Islamic philosopher from present-day Pakistan. Recognized as a leading liberal reformer within Islam, he focused on educational reform and promoting independent reasoning (ijtihad). His work has attracted both significant interest and criticism in Muslim-majority countries. His reformist ideas led to protests by over a thousand clerics, faqihs, muftis, and teachers in Pakistan, ultimately resulting in his exile.
After teaching in the UK and in Canada, where he formed a close friendship with philosopher Ismail al-Faruqi, Fazlur Rahman was appointed head of Pakistan’s Central Institute of Islamic Research in 1962. While widely respected among Islamic reformers, his ideas drew strong criticism from conservative scholars who viewed his approach as excessively liberal. Political opponents of his ally, General Ayub Khan, capitalized on this dissent, ultimately leading to Fazlur Rahman’s departure from Pakistan in 1968. He relocated to the United States, where he taught at the University of California, Los Angeles and later at the University of Chicago.

Biography

Early life and education
Fazlur Rahman was born in the Hazara District of the North West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) of British India (now Pakistan). His father, Maulana Shihab al-Din, was a prominent scholar who had studied at Deoband and held the title of alim through his expertise in Islamic law, prophetic narrations, Quranic commentaries, logic, philosophy, and other subjects. Under his father’s influence, Fazlur Rahman was introduced to traditional Islamic sciences and completed the memorization of the Quran at the age of ten. He pursued formal studies in Arabic at Punjab University, and later completed his doctoral studies at Oxford University, where he wrote a dissertation on Ibn Sina.

Early career
After completing his studies, Fazlur Rahman began his teaching career, initially at Durham University, where he taught Persian and Islamic philosophy. He later joined McGill University, where he taught Islamic studies until 1961. During his time at McGill, he formed a close association with the Palestinian-American philosopher Ismail al-Faruqi, introduced through Wilfred Cantwell Smith, the founder of McGill’s Institute of Islamic Studies. Under Smith’s mentorship, al-Faruqi delved deeply into Christian and Jewish theological studies, with Fazlur Rahman observing that Smith's guidance significantly shaped al-Faruqi’s comparative approach to religious studies and interfaith dialogue.

Return to Pakistan
In 1961, Fazlur Rahman returned to Pakistan at the request of President Ayub Khan to lead the Central Institute of Islamic Research in Karachi, which had been established by the Pakistani government to integrate Islamic principles into the nation’s public affairs. He also supported a two-year appointment for al-Faruqi at the Institute, where al-Faruqi served as a visiting professor. Reflecting on this period, Fazlur Rahman noted that the experience broadened al-Faruqi’s understanding of cultural diversity within Islam, ultimately shaping his approach to comparative religion and meta-religion. Despite his efforts, the political climate in Pakistan presented significant obstacles to Fazlur Rahman’s vision. Orthodox ulema opposed his modernist interpretations, and as Ayub Khan’s political influence waned. He ultimately resigned from the position in September 1968 and relocated to the United States.

Career in the United States
In the United States, Fazlur Rahman resumed his teaching career, first as a visiting professor at UCLA for a year. In 1969, he joined the University of Chicago, where he became the Harold H. Swift Distinguished Service Professor of Islamic Thought. At Chicago, he played an instrumental role in building a strong Near Eastern Studies program, which continues to be highly regarded. Fazlur Rahman also advocated for reform within Islamic governance and served as an advisor to the State Department. 
He died in Chicago, Illinois on July 26, 1988, at the University of Chicago Medical Center due to complications from coronary bypass surgery. At the time of his death, he was a resident of suburban Naperville, Illinois and is buried in Arlington Cemetery, Elmhurst, Illinois.

Legacy
Since Fazlur Rahman’s death, his writings have remained influential among scholars of Islam and the Near East in various countries, including Pakistan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Turkey, and the Arab region. His impact at the University of Chicago endures, particularly within its programs related to Islamic and Near Eastern studies. In his honor, the Center for Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Chicago named its common area after him, recognizing his many years of service and contributions to the university. A polyglot, he mastered Urdu, Persian, Arabic, and English early in life and later learned classical Greek, Latin, German, and French to further his academic work.

Views
Fazlur Rahman’s philosophy emphasized a return to the intellectual dynamism of early Islam, advocating a dynamic approach to religious interpretation. He believed in integrating philosophy, ethics, and rational thought to address contemporary issues facing the Muslim world. Fazlur Rahman criticized traditional Muslim theologies for overlooking the Quran’s moral principles, stressing that "moral values" endure beyond history and require constant reinterpretation. His work Islam and Modernity (1982) outline these ideas seeking to reconcile Islamic principles with modern challenges.

Social justice
Fazlur Rahman argued that Islamic tradition often prioritized judicial codes over developing a Quran-based ethical framework. Viewing historical Islamic governance models, such as the caliphate, as past solutions for societal justice, he called for a reformed understanding of justice rooted in the Quranic concept of shura (consultation). He proposed expanding shura to involve all levels of society, advocating collaboration between religious and secular scholars to address social justice issues.

Riba' and economic reform
Addressing riba (interest), Fazlur Rahman diverged from the strict prohibition stance of many Islamic revivalist movements. He contended that the Quran’s condemnation of riba referred specifically to exploitative, compounding interest in pre-Islamic Arabia, not moderate loan interest. Fazlur Rahman cited the Muwatta of Imam Malik to support his view, arguing for a nuanced interpretation that bans predatory lending while allowing interest in modern banking. This perspective directly opposed figures like Abul A'la Maududi, who advocated a total ban on interest. He wrote that “the initial interest itself was not usurious and was, therefore, not considered riba. What made it riba was the increase … that raised the principal several-fold by continued redoubling.”

Reform movements and intellectual revival
Fazlur Rahman was critical of both revivalist and modernist Islamic movements. He argued that 18th- and 19th-century revivalists stifled intellectual growth, while modernists selectively applied Islamic principles without grounding them in a robust methodology. Instead, he championed a "neo-modernism" rooted in a disciplined Islamic framework, advocating for a revival of rational inquiry within Islamic scholarship. His "double movement theory" reflects this approach by encouraging a balanced interpretation of Islamic teachings through context and present-day application, which has been highlighted as essential to fostering religious moderation.

Contextual interpretation of the Quran
Fazlur Rahman contributed significantly to the development of a contextual approach to examining the Qur’an, arguing that readers must consider both the historical context in which the text was revealed and contemporary social changes.

rows.name: Sabahattin Zaim
rows.key_contribution: Turkish Islamic economics; participation banking.
rows.bio_full: Sabahattin Zaim was born in 1926 in the town of Stip in Macedonia. He went to Fethiye Primary School in Fatih, Istanbul, and finished Vefa High School with a certificate of excellence. He graduated from the Faculty of Political Sciences of Ankara University in 1947, and also completed the university's Law Faculty. After graduating he worked as a head official in several districts. In 1953 he joined Istanbul University's Faculty of Economics as an assistant. He received his doctorate in 1955. From 1955 to 1957 he was a guest academic at Cornell University. He was promoted to professor in 1965. He stayed on the staff of Istanbul University until 1993. His books include Çalışma Ekonomisi (1968), on labour economics, and Modern İktisat ve İslâm (1969). Later titles on Islam and economics include İslâm’ın İktisadî Görüşü (1981) and İslâm, İnsan ve Ekonomi (1992). The encyclopaedia entry counts him among the first to bring Islamic economics to Turkey. He was deputy chairman of the First World Congress of Islamic Economics, held in Mecca in 1976. He sat on the board of trustees of Middle East Technical University from 1977 to 1979. From 1980 to 1982 he lectured at King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah. From 1995 he was a consultant to Kuveyt-Türk Finans Kurumu, an interest-free finance house, and sat on its audit board. From 1993 to 1998 he was dean of the Faculty of Economics and Administrative Sciences at Sakarya University, which he helped set up. He was a member of Turkey's Higher Education Council from 1998 to 2000. In 2003 and 2004 he was founding rector of the International University of Sarajevo. He was a founding member of the İlim Yayma Vakfı (Knowledge Dissemination Foundation). One encyclopaedia entry credits him with 20 books and 174 articles. His students included Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Abdullah Gül. The university that bears his name gives his date of death as 10 December 2007, at the age of 81. An encyclopaedia entry puts his death in Istanbul on 9 December 2007. He was buried in the family plot at Edirnekapı cemetery. The university founded in 2010 by the İlim Yayma Vakfı was named after him.

rows.bio_full: Muhammad Abdul Mannan was born on 10 January 1938 in a village in Sirajganj. He passed his matriculation at Victoria High School in Sirajganj in 1954 and his intermediate examination at Sirajganj College in 1956. He took a BA (Honours) in 1959 and a master's degree in economics at Rajshahi University in 1960. In August 1960 he began teaching as a lecturer at Sirajganj College. In 1963 he entered the East Pakistan Civil Service as a deputy magistrate. In 1967 he published a book on Pakistan's economic problems and planning. His book Islamic Economics: Theory and Practice was published in Lahore in 1970. The book was later revised and has been reprinted more than twenty times. He enrolled at Michigan State University in 1970 and received his doctorate there in 1973. In 1974 he left the United States to work at the Papua New Guinea University of Technology. From 1978 to 1982 he was a professor of economics and Islamic finance at King Abdul Aziz University in Jeddah. In 1982 he moved to the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah, where he worked as an economist and chaired the committee that prepared the bank's prize. He took early retirement from the bank in 1996 and returned to Bangladesh. He had a key part in setting up a bank in Bangladesh that opened on 22 November 1995 as Social Investment Bank and was later renamed Social Islami Bank Limited. Under his initiative that bank issued a cash waqf certificate. A later journal study describes this cash waqf scheme as an interest-free way of giving small loans. The same study says he set out a three-sector model, formal, informal and voluntary, for reducing poverty and inequality. It also discusses his views on consumption, production and distribution in an Islamic economy. In 2004 he set up a charitable trust in his family's name that runs education, health and welfare programmes. He received an award described as the highest academic award of Pakistan for his work on Islamic economics. He died on 31 March 2021, aged 83, in a Dhaka hospital where he was being treated for heart problems.

An older book listing describes him as a principal financial officer in the World Bank Treasury and as adjunct faculty in international finance at George Washington University. His work covers capital markets, asset management and risk management, and he has co-written articles and books on Islamic finance. He then became Vice President, Finance, and Chief Financial Officer of the Islamic Development Bank. In that post he spoke on capital markets at an Islamic finance conference in Kazakhstan on 27 June 2022, noting the bank's green sukuk listed there.

rows.name: Tariqullah Khan
rows.key_contribution: Risk management and financial engineering.
rows.bio_full: Tariqullah Khan was a BA student at Sindh Muslim College in Karachi in 1971-72, studying economics, political science and Islamic history. He began his academic career at Gomal University in Pakistan, where he worked from 1976 to 1981. From 1981 to 1983 he was at the International Islamic University Islamabad, in its school of Islamic economics. From 1983 to 2009 he worked as a researcher at the Islamic Research and Training Institute of the Islamic Development Bank Group. From 2005 to 2009 he was the institute's division chief for Islamic banking and finance. From 2009 to 2020 he was professor and programme director for Islamic finance at Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar. He was president of the International Association for Islamic Economics from 2011 to 2019. He was a visiting scholar at Harvard University in 2011 and at Stanford University in 2017. After Qatar he became professor of Islamic economics and finance at Istanbul Zaim University in Turkey. He has written papers, book chapters and books. He argues that meeting the halal test is required but is not enough on its own. He holds that the growth of finance for its own sake has pulled Islamic economics away from its purpose. He calls for Islamic finance to take up a circular, low-waste economic model, and for charitable endowments to work alongside commercial Islamic finance, for example by lowering the cost of funding. He also asks for the teaching of Islamic finance to be reformed. In May 2022 he won the third prize of the Islamic Development Bank Prize for Impactful Achievement in Islamic Economics. The prize announcement says he brought together the aims of Islamic economics and finance, the objectives of the Sharia and the Sustainable Development Goals, and brought the circular economy idea into Islamic economics.

rows.name: Rodney Wilson
rows.key_contribution: Pioneered Islamic finance academic study in the West.
rows.bio_full: Rodney Wilson is a British economist who, according to Wikipedia, was born in Belfast in 1946. He was employed at Durham University from October 1973 to December 2011. Wikipedia describes him as an emeritus professor of economics at Durham. He started research on Islamic finance at Durham in the mid-1990s. He helped to set up Durham's master's course in Islamic finance. At Durham he served as director of postgraduate studies in his school, taught master's courses on Islamic economics and finance, and supervised doctoral students. His 1997 book Economics, Ethics and Religion compared the ethical basis of economic thought in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. His other books include Economic Development in the Middle East (1995), The Politics of Islamic Finance (as editor, 2004), Islamic Finance in Europe (2007) and Islam and Economic Policy: An Introduction (2020). In a 2009 article he argued that Islamic financial firms need extra layers of rules to deal with governance and risk. The Islamic Financial Services Board brought him in during 2009. He attended five meetings of its working group on Sharia governance and helped to write its guiding principles on Sharia governance systems. He chaired the academic committee of the Institute of Islamic Banking and Insurance in London. He did consultancy work for the Islamic Development Bank in Jeddah and for the Ministry of Economy and Planning in Riyadh. From 2008 he gave regular training courses for firms and professionals. In 2014 he shared the Islamic Development Bank prize in Islamic banking and finance with Muhammad Taqi Usmani of Pakistan. The prize committee cited his long record of teaching, research, supervision and consultancy, and his part in bringing Islamic finance courses into universities in Britain and Europe.

rows.name: Ungku Abdul Aziz (Ungku Aziz)
rows.key_contribution: Conceived Tabung Haji (Pilgrims Fund).
rows.bio_full: Ungku Abdul Aziz was born in Hampstead, London, on 28 January 1922. He was schooled at the English College in Johor Bahru and at a Malay school in Batu Pahat. He received a diploma in arts from Raffles College in Singapore. In 1951 he took a bachelor's degree in economics at the University of Malaya. He worked for a time in the Johor state administration. From 1952 to 1961, with a one-year break, he lectured at the University of Malaya in Singapore. In 1956-57 he headed Malaysia's council on language and literature. On 30 September 1959 he sent the government a paper on how to improve the way would-be pilgrims saved for the hajj. He proposed that Muslims save with a body that followed Islamic law, which would also arrange their pilgrimage and pay returns free of interest. The pilgrims' savings body that grew from this idea is dated by Wikipedia to 30 September 1963; it was merged with the hajj affairs office in 1969 and took the short name Lembaga Tabung Haji in 1995. A national newspaper obituary says he was instrumental in setting up the pilgrims' fund board. From 1962 to 1965 he was professor and dean of the economics faculty of the University of Malaya in Kuala Lumpur. He defended a doctoral thesis at Waseda University in Tokyo in 1964. He was Vice-Chancellor of the University of Malaya from 1968 to 1988, the first Malaysian in the post and the one who served longest. In 1978 he was given the title of Royal Professor. His research dealt with rural poverty, rural development and land tenure, including the breaking-up of rubber estates at the end of colonial rule. He wrote more than fifty books and monographs on Malaysia's social and economic problems. He was president of Malaysia's national cooperative organisation and helped to found the Malaysian Economics Association. His daughter, Zeti Akhtar Aziz, was governor of Malaysia's central bank. He died in hospital in Kuala Lumpur on 15 December 2020, aged 98.

rows.name: al-Quduri
rows.key_contribution: His best-known book is the Mukhtasar, a short manual of Hanafi law.
rows.bio_full: Abu al-Husayn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan al-Quduri was a Hanafi jurist of Baghdad. He was born in 362 AH. The classical biographers give the same year. English Wikipedia converts this to 972 or 973 CE and gives Baghdad as his birthplace. He learned law from Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Jurjani. He became the head of the Hanafi school in Iraq. Those who studied law with him include Abu Nasr al-Aqta', who wrote a commentary on his short manual. Those who passed on reports from him include al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, the historian of Baghdad, and the chief judge Abu Abd Allah al-Damaghani. His best-known book is the Mukhtasar, a short manual of Hanafi law. He also wrote a commentary on the Mukhtasar of al-Karkhi. Another of his works is al-Tajrid, in seven parts, which English Wikipedia describes as comparing Hanafi and Shafi'i positions. Arabic Wikipedia also lists a book called al-Taqrib. He died in Baghdad in the month of Rajab 428 AH, aged sixty-six. One classical entry puts the death on a Sunday in the middle of Rajab. Another puts it on Sunday the fifth of Rajab. English Wikipedia gives the year as 1036/1037 CE in one place and the date 24 April 1037 in another. He was buried the same day in his house in Darb Abi Khalaf, and his remains were later moved to a tomb on al-Mansur street.
